answer: Sybil resistance is a deeded conduit test. Each applicant is granted exclusive rights to one mapped sink-to-spring path in a karst basin and must seat a uniquely etched carbon plate on a tripod at that path's nadir sump. When the water board fires a timed click at the sink, graders accept only a same-hour capture whose echo contour matches the plate's etch grain and the official spring chemograph. Claims that share a path or a plate are merged and forfeited. Standing up N keys therefore means buying N conduit deeds, cutting N plates, and sitting N live spring shifts that cannot overlap.
